questions.question: What is a brute force strategy?
options: An approach that skips invalid inputs to save time
A method that uses mathematical shortcuts to find answers instantly
An approach that systematically tries every possible candidate solution until the correct one is found
A technique that divides the problem into subproblems and solves each independently
questions.explanation: Brute force exhaustively tries all possibilities without applying any optimization or pruning, guaranteeing correctness at the cost of efficiency.

questions.question: Why is brute force inefficient for large inputs?
options: Because it always produces incorrect results for large datasets
Because the number of operations grows too fast (often O(n²) or worse), making it impractical for large n
Because it requires special hardware to run correctly
Because it cannot be implemented using block-based programming
questions.explanation: Brute force often has polynomial or exponential time complexity, causing execution time to explode as input size increases — making it infeasible for large-scale problems.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of this search function?
options: O(1) — returns immediately when found
O(log n) — skips half the array each step
O(n) — must scan all n elements if target is absent or at the last index
O(n²) — compares every pair of elements
questions.explanation: In the worst case (target not found), the loop iterates through all n elements before returning -1 — this is O(n) linear search.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of linear search?
options: O(1) — constant time
O(log n) — logarithmic time
O(n) — linear time
O(n²) — quadratic time
questions.explanation: Linear search is O(n) because in the worst case it must examine every element in the array once.

questions.question: Does linear search require sorted data?
options: Yes, it only works on ascending sorted arrays
Yes, it requires either ascending or descending sorted data
No, it works on both sorted and unsorted data
No, but it produces incorrect results on unsorted data
questions.explanation: Linear search works by sequentially checking each element, so it does not require the data to be sorted — unlike Binary Search.

questions.question: What are the time and space complexities of this function?
options: Time: O(n²), Space: O(n)
Time: O(log n), Space: O(1)
Time: O(n), Space: O(1) — scans all elements once, uses only one extra variable
Time: O(1), Space: O(n)
questions.explanation: The loop visits each of the n elements exactly once → O(n) time. Only max_val is allocated as extra storage regardless of input size → O(1) space.

questions.question: What is Bubble Sort?
options: A sorting algorithm that selects the minimum element and places it at the front
A sorting algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are in the wrong order until the array is sorted
A sorting algorithm that divides the array in half recursively and merges sorted halves
A sorting algorithm that inserts elements one by one into their correct position
questions.explanation: Bubble Sort works by repeatedly comparing and swapping adjacent elements, causing larger elements to 'bubble' toward the end with each pass.

questions.question: What is Selection Sort?
options: A sorting algorithm that swaps adjacent elements in each pass
A sorting algorithm that repeatedly finds the minimum element from the unsorted portion and places it at the beginning of the unsorted region
A sorting algorithm that uses a pivot to partition elements
A sorting algorithm that merges two halves into a sorted array
questions.explanation: Selection Sort scans the unsorted portion for the minimum element and swaps it into its correct position, expanding the sorted portion one element at a time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of this Bubble Sort implementation?
options: O(n) — only the outer loop is counted
O(n log n) — inner loop halves each pass
O(n²) — outer loop runs n times and inner loop runs ~n times for each outer iteration
O(2n) — two loops added together
questions.explanation: Two nested loops each running ~n times gives n × n = n² comparisons in the worst case — classic O(n²) for simple sorting algorithms like Bubble Sort.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Selection Sort?
options: O(n) in all cases
O(n log n) in the best case
O(n²) in all cases, because it always scans the full unsorted portion
O(log n) for small arrays
questions.explanation: Selection Sort is always O(n²) — even if the array is already sorted, it must still scan the full unsorted portion to confirm the minimum element.

questions.question: Why do simple sorting algorithms use nested loops?
options: Because nested loops are required by the Python programming language
To process each element, they must compare it with every other relevant element, requiring an outer loop for passes and an inner loop for comparisons
Because single loops are not powerful enough to store sorted results
Nested loops are only used for printing 2D grids, not for sorting
questions.explanation: Simple O(n²) sorts use an outer loop to iterate over positions and an inner loop to find the correct element or make comparisons — this double iteration causes the quadratic complexity.

questions.question: Comparing space complexity: which version uses less memory and why?
options: Version B — slicing is always more memory efficient
Version A — it modifies the array in-place using only two pointer variables, O(1) extra space vs Version B's O(n) for the new array
They are equal — both operate on the same array
Version A — recursion uses less space than slicing
questions.explanation: Version A swaps in-place using only two integer pointer variables → O(1) extra space. Version B creates a completely new reversed array → O(n) extra space.

questions.question: How do you find the maximum value in an unsorted array?
options: By jumping directly to the middle element
By sorting the array first, then reading the last element
By iterating through every element and tracking the largest value seen so far
By using binary search on the unsorted array
questions.explanation: Without sorting, the only reliable way to find the maximum is to scan all elements linearly while maintaining a running maximum — a classic O(n) brute force approach.

questions.question: Is brute force acceptable here, and what is the time complexity?
options: No — brute force is never acceptable even for small inputs
Yes — the input is small (n=10), so O(n) linear scan completes instantly and simplicity outweighs optimization need
No — this should use binary search for O(log n)
Yes — but only because the list is already sorted
questions.explanation: For very small fixed inputs like n=10, the O(n) brute force scan finishes in microseconds. The cost of implementing a more complex algorithm far exceeds any performance benefit.

questions.question: What is an auxiliary array?
options: The original input array passed to a function
An array that stores only negative values
A temporary additional array used to assist the main algorithm, typically to store intermediate results
An array that is automatically created by the programming language runtime
questions.explanation: An auxiliary array is a helper data structure used alongside the main data to store intermediate values — for example, a seen-values array used to track visited elements in O(n) duplicate detection.
